title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review Standards, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary
This page defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and runbook conventions. The goal is to ensure consistent, measurable reliability across hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments while enabling rapid, blameless incident response.

Scope
Applies to all customer-facing runtime services (example service names: redwood-inference-api, runtime-gateway, batching-service, kvcache, routing-service) and control-plane components used in production. Internal developer tools should follow the same principles where applicable.

1) SLO and Error Budget Standards
- SLO types: availability (successful request rate), latency (p50/p95/p99), and correctness (model quality regressions tied to evaluation suites).
- Default SLOs (starting point):
  - redwood-inference-api (hosted): availability 99.95% monthly; p99 latency <= 250ms for short completions (<=512 tokens); p95 latency <= 120ms.
  - runtime-gateway: availability 99.99% monthly; p99 latency <= 50ms.
  - batch-embedding-service: availability 99.9% monthly; throughput SLO: 10k embeddings/min sustained per reserved cluster unit.
- Error budget definitions: error budget = 1 - SLO over the relevant burn window (monthly default). Errors include 5xx responses, client-visible timeouts, and recorded model-quality regression failures if tied to a rollout.
- Burn policy:
  - Alert at 25% of budget consumed (notify service owner and on-call).
  - Mitigation required at 50% consumption for 24h sustained burn (owner must open a mitigation plan in PagerDuty incident and document actions).
  - Emergency freeze at >= 100% consumption: immediate rollback of non-critical rollouts, suspend risky deployments, and engage incident review.
- Ownership: each service must have an SLO owner (primary and secondary) listed in the service registry. SLO owner is responsible for SLO definition, monitoring, and error budget actions.

2) SLO Measurement and Observability
- Metric sources: Prometheus metrics (request_success_count, request_total, request_latency_seconds_bucket), tracing via OpenTelemetry, and application logs indexed in Loki/Elasticsearch.
- Calculation: use Prometheus recording rules to compute rolling-window SLOs (30d and 7d) and a monthly window. Include partial-window correction for new services.
- Dashboards: every SLO must have a Grafana dashboard with: current SLO, burn rate chart, latency percentiles, traffic volume, error breakdown (5xx vs timeouts).
- Alerts: PagerDuty for owner on 25%/50%/100% thresholds, Slack channel notifications for 10% increments.

3) Capacity Planning and Scaling
- Forecasting cadence: quarterly capacity review and monthly health review. Capacity owners must produce a 90/180/365-day forecast including: traffic growth, model changes (larger context or parameter increases), and known upcoming customers/features.
- KPIs used for planning: average QPS, peak QPS (99.9th percentile), p99 tail latency, GPU utilization (per-cluster), queue length, and KV cache hit rate.
- Safety margin: production pools must target 25% headroom on typical peak to allow for autoscaling buffer and regional failover. Critical (SLA-backed) customers may require dedicated pools with 10% headroom SLA commitment.
- Autoscaling policies: recommend HPA-like autoscaling for service pods and autoscaler for GPU workers with min/max and cool-down periods documented. Default scale-up triggers: CPU>70% for 3m or queue length > threshold; scale-down only after 10m of sustained low usage.
- Capacity runbook (summary):
  1. Identify impacted cluster and service from dashboards.
  2. Check autoscaler status and recent scaling events.
  3. If autoscaler saturated, open capacity request ticket to infra with priority and expected duration.
  4. Apply temporary routing policy (route to dedicated pool or increase burst capacity) and document change in incident notes.

4) Reliability Initiatives and Investment Prioritization
- Annual reliability program: services with >3 incidents crossing S1/S2 in 90 days must be flagged for reliability initiative. Initiative includes: focused engineering time (2-4 sprint weeks), targeted load testing, and post-initiative SLO review.
- Continuous improvement: prioritize fixes that reduce error budget burn or materially increase capacity efficiency (batching improvements, KV cache efficiency, kernel selection optimization).
- Measurement: track ROI of reliability work via reduced error budget consumption, lower incident count, and improved cost-per-token.

5) Incident Review and Postmortem Standards
- Severity classification: S1 (service down/large user impact), S2 (partial outage/degraded latency affecting many customers), S3 (minor degradation/limited impact).
- Timelines: postmortem draft due within 72 hours of incident mitigation; final postmortem published within 10 business days.
- Postmortem template (must be used):
  - Summary: one-line description and impact scope.
  - Timeline: 1-minute resolution timeline of events.
  - Root cause: clear technical root cause statement.
  - Contributing factors: list of systemic or process issues.
  - Detection: how was the incident detected (alert name, paging).
  - Mitigation and remediation: what was done to restore service and permanent fixes planned.
  - Action items: owner, due date, and verification steps.
  - Learnings: what to change in runbooks, monitoring, or architecture.
- Blamelessness: focus on systemic fixes, not individual blame. Reviewers must include the SLO owner, on-call responder, and an independent reviewer from another SRE/Platform team.

6) Operational Tooling and Playbooks
- Standard dashboards: SLO overview, capacity heatmap, regional failover status, and deployment health. Templates are in /eng-sre/dashboards-and-alerts.
- Alert hygiene: every alert must have: purpose, owner, actionable next steps, and runbook link. Avoid high-noise alerts; aim for <2 actionable pages per on-call per week.
- On-call rotations: 2-week rotations recommended with 2 responders (primary + secondary). Escalation chain integrates PagerDuty to on-call, then team lead, then platform SRE.
- Runbook format and storage: YAML front-matter metadata is required for automation; content stored in Confluence and mirrored to repo: infra/runbooks/ as markdown. Example metadata fields: service, owner, severity, last_tested, playbook_version.

7) Runbook Conventions (template and example)
- Each runbook must include: purpose, pre-req checks, detection indicators, step-by-step mitigation (numbered), rollback steps for recent changes, communication templates (customer and internal), and verification steps.
- Example quick mitigation for API 5xx surge:
  1. Verify the alert: grafana alert "redwood-api-5xx-rate" triggered.
  2. Identify service instances with high error rate: kubectl -n prod logs --selector app=redwood-inference-api | grep 5xx.
  3. Check recent deploys: gitlab-ci release pipeline and deployment timestamps.
  4. If recent rollout suspected, rollback to previous canary: kubectl rollout undo deployment/redwood-inference-api --to-revision=<rev>.
  5. If capacity issue: increase burst capacity or switch routing to dedicated pool: /ops/routing set-route --service redwood-inference-api --pool dedicated-pool-1 --priority override.
  6. Notify customers (template available) and update incident notes.

8) Verification and Testing
- Runbook drills: quarterly game-days to exercise critical runbooks (failover, rollback, capacity surge). Each drill must generate a drill report and update runbooks where steps failed or were unclear.
- SLO and alert testing: synthetic tests must run every 1m for critical endpoints; results feed into SLO dashboards for early detection of regressions.

9) Roles and Responsibilities
- SLO Owner: defines SLOs, creates dashboards, owns error budget actions and mitigation plans.
- Service Owner (team): maintenance, reliability initiatives, and capacity forecast.
- Platform SRE: tools, autoscaling policies, and cross-service reliability frameworks.
- Incident Commander (IC): runs incident until service restored and hands off to postmortem owner.

10) Governance and Review Cadence
- Quarterly SLO review meeting: each service owner presents SLO health, error budget usage, and planned reliability initiatives.
- Annual audit: Security & Compliance may audit SLOs and runbooks for enterprise customers (Private deployments).

Appendices
A. Example Prometheus rule (SLO availability)
  - record: job:slo:availability
    expr: (sum(rate(request_success_count[5m])) / sum(rate(request_total[5m])))

B. Communication templates: incident-summary, customer-notice, mitigation-plan (stored in /eng-sre/templates).

C. Useful links
- Service registry: /internal/service-registry
- SRE dashboards: /grafana/dashboards/sre-slos-overview
